title: Evaluating Evaluators: Meta-Benchmark for Safety Autograder Accuracy on Edge Cases

original_idea.title: Evaluating Evaluators: Meta-Benchmark for Safety Autograder Accuracy on Edge Cases
original_idea.problem: LLM judges are increasingly used to automate safety evaluation, but their accuracy on edge cases -- responses that are borderline harmful, satirical, or context-dependent -- is poorly characterized.
original_idea.direction: Construct a meta-benchmark of 50-80 edge-case model responses with high human annotator disagreement (collected via a small annotation task). Evaluate 3 LLM judges on these edge cases. Compute judge accuracy against majority human vote, inter-judge agreement, and consistency across repeated runs. Report which categories of edge cases are most problematic for automated judges.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Edge cases are where automated evaluation fails most critically. A meta-benchmark specifically designed around high-disagreement items provides a rigorous test of autograder limits.
original_idea.relevant_context: RAND's Judge Reliability Harness (2025) tests judge reliability broadly. AISI's Skewed Score paper provides statistical tools. This experiment focuses specifically on the hardest-to-judge safety cases.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Reduced from 4 to 3. Multiple concurrent works (RAND JRH, Know Thy Judge, Safer or Luckier) already address autograder reliability, reducing the marginal impact of this contribution.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: constructing edge cases and running annotation tasks requires careful methodology, but the technical components (LLM API calls, agreement metrics) are manageable for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: a 50-80 item meta-benchmark with judge accuracy metrics and category-level analysis. Clear endpoint.

novelty.reasoning: This space is actively researched. RAND's Judge Reliability Harness (2026) is an end-to-end framework for stress-testing LLM judges. 'Know Thy Judge' (ICLR 2025 Workshop) demonstrated that small style changes cause false negative rate jumps of up to 0.24. 'Safer or Luckier?' (ACL 2025) showed apologetic language artifacts skew evaluator preferences by up to 98%. JudgeBench provides high-difficulty response pairs for evaluating judges. The specific focus on human-annotated high-disagreement safety edge cases is a valid angle, but the broader 'evaluating evaluators' direction is already partially addressed by multiple concurrent works.
